The question of when the Spaniards and Portuguese drove out the Moorish Arabs does not have a single universally agreed-upon answer, as the timelines differ for Spain and Portugal and depend on how "driven out" is defined. For Spain, d7 (Britannica) and d3 both identify 1492 as the decisive year, when Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile completed the conquest of Granada — the last Moorish stronghold — ending nearly 800 years of Islamic rule on the Iberian Peninsula [d7][d3]. For Portugal, d7 notes that Afonso III captured Faro in 1249, "the last Moorish stronghold in the Algarve," effectively ending Portugal's reconquest by the end of the 13th century [d7]; d2 similarly states that the Portuguese reconquest "ended in the 13th century" [d2]. However, d6 (Wikipedia) complicates the picture by noting that Moorish presence and forced conversions continued well into the 16th century, with Holy Roman Emperor Charles V imposing mandatory conversion on Moors in Aragon as late as 1526 [d6]. Thus, while 1492 is the most commonly cited year for Spain's expulsion of the Moors, Portugal's reconquest concluded around 1249, and the full cultural and religious suppression of Moorish communities extended into the 1500s [d7][d6][d2].
